questions.question: In asthma, which of the following is NOT a possible risk factor for death?
questions.exp: Regular inhaled steroids protect against asthma death. Over-use of reliever, previous admissions and psychosocial problems are risk factors.

questions.question: At what age can a young person give full consent for research purposes?
questions.exp: Full independent consent for research is taken at 18 (adult age); younger children give assent with parental consent.

questions.question: Which sign indicates airway narrowing?
questions.exp: Wheeze is the musical sound of narrowed intrathoracic airways.

questions.question: Of 100 children with UTI, the dipstick is positive in 90 and negative in 10. Of 100 children without UTI, it is negative in 90 and positive in 10. What is the sensitivity of the dipstick?
questions.exp: Sensitivity = true positives / all with disease = 90/100 = 90%. (Specificity here is also 90%.)

questions.question: A 26-week preterm neonate in NICU was stable, then develops bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and bloody diarrhoea. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Prematurity with distension, bilious aspirates and bloody stool is NEC.

questions.question: A girl has linear streaky lesions on her back along Blaschko lines that became warty. Which cells are responsible for the lesion?
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti (NEMO mutation): vesicular, then verrucous, then hyperpigmented stages from keratinocyte apoptosis.

questions.question: A boy has fatigue, poor feeding, left-sided chest pain and tachycardia. His mother has SLE. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Serositis (pericarditis) is the commonest cardiac manifestation of lupus. The recall keyed pericarditis.

questions.question: Which vaccines are given to an 8-week-old baby?
questions.exp: UK-style 8-week schedule: 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB), rotavirus and MenB.

questions.question: A baby can roll over, recognises their name and sits with support but is not yet steady. What is the age?
questions.exp: Rolling and sitting with support (tripod, unsteady) and turning to name are 6-month milestones.

questions.question: Triage vitals for an infant were HR 170, RR 45, temperature 37 °C. When the doctor saw the infant, all vitals were normal. What is the explanation?
questions.exp: An upset or crying infant has a transient sinus tachycardia that settles at rest.

questions.question: An infant comes to ER with circumoral cyanosis only. What oxygen saturation would you expect on the probe?
questions.exp: Circumoral (perioral) blueness alone is usually benign or mild; central cyanosis appears below about 85%. The recall keyed 89% but was unsure.

questions.question: In a child with nephrotic syndrome, which antibody status is most important to screen for infection before steroids?
questions.exp: Check varicella immunity: non-immune children on steroids need VZIG/aciclovir after exposure.

questions.question: A child with leukaemia on cyclophosphamide develops haematuria. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Acrolein from cyclophosphamide causes haemorrhagic cystitis; prevented by hydration and mesna.

questions.question: Jaundice beyond 2 weeks of life can be due to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: ABO haemolysis causes early jaundice (first 24 hours), not prolonged jaundice.

questions.question: A child had brain-stem death after an accident and the team decided to withdraw life support. The parents agree but the grandparents disagree. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Parents hold parental responsibility; decisions are made with them.
questions.d: Agree with the grandparents and continue support

questions.question: A child has stable SVT. What is the first step?
questions.exp: Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres first, then adenosine.

questions.question: A baby has a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. What is the lesion?
questions.exp: Pansystolic murmur at LLSE = VSD.

questions.question: A baby has a continuous machinery murmur with a thrill and is not gaining weight. What is the best action?
questions.exp: A haemodynamically significant PDA (failure to thrive) needs closure; the recall keyed referral. Diuretics are supportive only.
questions.b: Refer to the paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon

questions.question: A child drinks too much cow's milk. What is he likely to be deficient in?
questions.exp: Excess cow's milk is low in iron, displaces solids and causes occult GI blood loss.

questions.question: A baby presents with umbilical bleeding. What is the most important point in the history?
questions.exp: Home births may have missed vitamin K: think vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
questions.c: Home delivery or not (vitamin K given?)

questions.question: A baby under 6 months comes to ER drowsy with multiple bruises. CT shows a subdural haematoma; the parents appear careless. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Stabilise first (ABC, raised ICP). Skeletal survey and safeguarding referral must follow but are not the immediate step.
questions.c: Admit to ICU and do a skeletal survey
questions.d: Admit to ICU and reduce intracranial pressure

questions.question: A child with URTI and nasal discharge develops painful periorbital oedema. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Suspected orbital cellulitis: CT of orbits and sinuses to look for abscess.

questions.question: A child pricked his hand on a plant tip, then developed facial swelling and began to suffocate. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.exp: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline (0.15 mg for under 6 years, 0.3 mg for 6–12 years).

questions.question: A child has atopic dermatitis with flexural rash. What is the best treatment to start with?
questions.exp: Emollients plus mild topical steroid first; step up as needed.

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis has abdominal pain, nausea and raised direct bilirubin. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: CF predisposes to gallstones and biliary disease, giving conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has reduced vision in one eye (possibly with squint). Examination shows retinal exudates. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: The recall keyed CMV chorioretinitis but the candidate did not remember the other options; Coats disease and toxocara also give unilateral exudates in young boys.

questions.question: Lesions along Blaschko lines are seen in which disease?
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti follows Blaschko lines.

questions.question: A child who has just started school has hair loss with a scaly red patch on the scalp. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Scaly patch with alopecia in a school child = tinea capitis (oral antifungal).

questions.question: A 14-year-old girl has had odynophagia for 4 years, especially for meat, with no problem with water. Examination is unremarkable, with no heartburn or regurgitation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: The recall keyed psychogenic. Note that solid-food dysphagia in an adolescent is classic for eosinophilic oesophagitis, which was not offered.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy develops involuntary hand and face movements and says inappropriate words after the loss of his close grandmother. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Motor plus vocal tics (including coprolalia) = Tourette syndrome; stress worsens tics.

questions.question: A toxic, febrile child has skin blisters; the skin peels easily when touched. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Positive Nikolsky sign with fever = SSSS.

questions.question: In a 6-month-old, persistence of which reflex suggests cerebral palsy?
questions.exp: Moro normally disappears by 4–6 months; persistence suggests CP.

questions.question: A child with Down syndrome has a single palmar crease and epicanthic folds. What is the most common type of mutation?
questions.exp: About 95% of Down syndrome is from maternal meiotic non-disjunction.

questions.question: What is the most common organism in early-onset neonatal sepsis?
questions.exp: GBS is the leading cause; E. coli is second (and leads in preterms).

questions.question: Regarding Bell's palsy, which statement is INCORRECT?
questions.exp: Bell's palsy is LMN and involves the forehead; forehead sparing indicates an UMN lesion. Facial palsy can occur with hypertension from coarctation.
questions.a: It can be associated with coarctation of the aorta
questions.b: It is a pure lower motor neurone lesion
questions.c: Most cases resolve within months without residue

questions.question: In atopic dermatitis, what is the first step in the mechanism?
questions.exp: Filaggrin-related barrier dysfunction comes first, then sensitisation.

questions.question: A boy has symptoms of hereditary angioedema and his mother has angioedema. Which is INCORRECT?
questions.exp: HAE is bradykinin-mediated (C1-INH deficiency) and is not allergic.
questions.a: It is caused by food allergy
questions.b: Attacks can be triggered by cold
questions.c: It is due to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency
questions.d: Attacks can be triggered by exercise

questions.question: What is the initial hearing screening test for a 2-day-old neonate?
questions.exp: Newborn screening starts with OAE; AABR follows if no clear response.

questions.question: All are examples of type III hypersensitivity EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The recall keyed extrinsic allergic alveolitis, but a reviewer noted it is classically type III (with type IV), so all three may be correct.

questions.question: A newborn with very high bilirubin starts to have seizures. What is the explanation?
questions.exp: Unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood–brain barrier and damages the basal ganglia.

questions.question: A newborn boy has a squint of the right eye and a white pupillary reflex. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Suspected retinoblastoma: urgent EUA and MRI. Biopsy is contraindicated (risk of seeding).

questions.question: A newborn boy has microphthalmia, undescended testes and cleft lip and palate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Trisomy 13: midline defects (cleft lip/palate), microphthalmia, polydactyly, cutis aplasia.

questions.question: A 2-year-old with eczema has fever and pustular, crusted lesions. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: The recall keyed oral aciclovir plus antibiotics (possible eczema herpeticum with staph superinfection). A febrile, unwell child with eczema herpeticum needs IV aciclovir.

questions.question: In DKA, fluid correction has started. What is the main danger of rapid correction?
questions.exp: Rapid fluid and sodium shifts risk cerebral oedema.

questions.question: A baby girl has a 1.5 cm area of aplasia cutis congenita on the scalp. Which statement is correct?
questions.exp: Small isolated lesions heal by themselves. Association with sebaceous/epidermal naevus syndrome brings seizures and CNS involvement.
questions.a: It is most probably Patau syndrome
questions.c: If associated with an epidermal naevus, the risk of seizures increases

questions.question: A girl has weakness, pain, cold extremities and severe fatigue on moving her limbs after infectious mononucleosis. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Post-viral (EBV) chronic fatigue syndrome. Reviewers were split between chronic fatigue and ongoing glandular fever.

questions.question: A newborn boy has cyanotic spells while feeding that resolve when he cries and turns pink again. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Bilateral choanal atresia: obligate nasal breathers turn blue when feeding and pink when crying.

questions.question: A toxic, febrile child has neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of acute kidney injury in children?
questions.exp: HUS is the commonest intrinsic cause of AKI in young children.

questions.question: A girl at routine follow-up has high TSH and height on the 0.4th centile; other parameters are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Short stature in a girl with autoimmune hypothyroidism suggests Turner syndrome: karyotype.

questions.question: A child arrested; CPR for 2 hours failed and was stopped. The parents object, saying CPR was poor quality, and start resuscitating the child themselves. Which ethical principle applies?
questions.exp: The recall keyed justice, with doubt. Stopping futile resuscitation is usually framed as non-maleficence and best interests.

questions.question: In suspected meningitis, which of the following is NOT appropriate?
questions.exp: A normal CRP or WBC does not exclude meningitis; suspected cases are admitted and treated.
questions.a: If CRP is negative and WBC low but bacterial meningitis is suspected, treat as bacterial
questions.b: If CRP is negative and WBC low, treat as herpetic or viral at home with OPD follow-up
questions.c: Do a lumbar puncture if no contraindication
questions.d: If CRP is positive and WBC high, treat as bacterial with ceftriaxone

questions.question: A 12-year-old with type 1 diabetes and fatigue has a random glucose of 18 mmol/L. What is the most useful action?
questions.exp: Optimise the basal-bolus regimen. Sulfonylureas have no role in type 1 diabetes.
questions.b: Target HbA1c above 6.5% to avoid complications

questions.question: A child presents with an abdominal mass and hemihypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hemihypertrophy (Beckwith–Wiedemann) predisposes to Wilms tumour.

questions.question: In HSP, which renal manifestation is most common?
questions.exp: Microscopic haematuria is the commonest renal finding in HSP.

questions.question: A child has purpuric rash on the buttocks and legs with haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Palpable purpura on the extensor lower limbs with haematuria = HSP (IgA vasculitis).

questions.question: In ALL, which of the following is a bad prognostic factor?
questions.exp: Poor prognosis: age under 1 or over 10, WBC above 50,000, T-cell, unfavourable cytogenetics. The recall keyed age above 10.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT predict that asthma will persist or be hard to treat?
questions.exp: The recall keyed house dust; atopy, allergic rhinitis and recurrent admissions predict persistent or difficult asthma.

questions.question: About RSV, which statement is WRONG?
questions.exp: RSV causes neutrophilic, not eosinophilic, inflammation. The recall's tick was unclear.
questions.d: It can cause persistent wheeze throughout infancy

questions.question: What is the most accurate test to diagnose congenital CMV?
questions.exp: Urine or saliva PCR in the first 21 days confirms congenital CMV.
questions.c: CMV PCR in urine (within 3 weeks of birth)

questions.question: A 10-year-old returns from holiday after an insect bite, with a circular target-like lesion on his chest. What is the best treatment?
questions.exp: Erythema migrans (Lyme disease): oral doxycycline (amoxicillin in younger children).

questions.question: A toddler drinks too much cow's milk and has iron deficiency anaemia. What is the best advice to the mother?
questions.exp: Limit cow's milk to about 500 mL/day, add iron-rich foods, give oral iron.
questions.b: Stop all milk and give other nutrients
questions.c: Reduce milk intake, give weaning foods and refer to a dietitian

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has leg pain and cannot bear weight; X-ray shows a small femoral head. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Sickle cell disease causes AVN of the femoral head.
questions.a: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (Perthes-like)

questions.question: A child fell off his bicycle with a 10 cm leg wound, now has severe pain, cannot bear weight and has pain on passive movement. What is expected on tibia and fibula X-ray?
questions.exp: Early osteomyelitis (or compartment syndrome): X-ray changes appear only after 10–14 days.
questions.c: Too early to see any changes

questions.question: Regarding renal imaging in a newborn with UTI, which is right?
questions.exp: NICE: atypical or recurrent UTI under 6 months needs ultrasound during the infection.
questions.a: DMSA during the acute infection for all
questions.c: A neonate with atypical UTI needs ultrasound during the acute illness

questions.question: A child has hyperkalaemia with ECG changes and calcium gluconate has been started. What is the most dangerous ECG sign?
questions.exp: A sine-wave pattern precedes VF or asystole.

questions.question: Regarding renal imaging, which is WRONG?
questions.exp: A ureterocele is usually associated with a duplex system on the same side.
questions.a: Dilatation of the renal pelvis suggests PUJ obstruction
questions.b: Marked bilateral ureteric dilatation suggests a ureterocele
questions.c: Thick bladder wall with mild bilateral ureteric dilatation suggests posterior urethral valves in males
questions.d: A single ureterocele suggests a duplex system on the contralateral side

questions.question: A newborn has a waiter's tip deformity. What is the best action?
questions.exp: The recall answer mentioned a fractured clavicle; waiter's tip is Erb palsy (C5–C6), which usually recovers with passive exercises.
questions.b: Reassure that it will recover with physiotherapy (Erb palsy)
questions.d: Splint the arm across the chest for 3 months

questions.question: Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC above 75% (a restrictive pattern). Which condition is NOT consistent with this result?
questions.exp: The recall is uncertain (above or below 75%). The keyed answer was cystic fibrosis.

questions.question: A girl brought by her grandmother for an infection is underweight and short for her age. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Faltering growth with concern for neglect: admit, assess and safeguard.
questions.a: Consider neglect, talk to the grandmother and give dietary advice
questions.b: Discharge with follow-up in a year
questions.c: Treat the infection and give a nutrition schedule

questions.question: A teenage girl with anorexia nervosa turned vegan: HR 40, low BP, weight dropped from 57 to 40 kg. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Bradycardia and hypotension are admission criteria for medical stabilisation and refeeding.
questions.a: Admit to detect the eating disorder

questions.question: A teenage girl with anorexia doing diet and exercise has TSH 7 and free T4 12.5 (normal 12). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: The recall was unsure; a reviewer noted subclinical hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid. Starvation changes thyroid tests (sick euthyroid).

questions.question: A teenager with anorexia nervosa is admitted for refeeding. What is the most significant finding to watch for?
questions.exp: Refeeding syndrome: low phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

questions.question: Which DDH test displaces the femoral head out of the acetabulum while holding and moving the leg?
questions.exp: Barlow dislocates; Ortolani relocates.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy is short compared with peers and has not entered puberty. His father had a 4-year delay in puberty. The boy is upset. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Likely constitutional delay: plot growth and puberty and reassess; consider a short testosterone course if distressed.
questions.b: Plot on growth charts and reassess
questions.d: Refer to adolescent medicine to assess his needs

questions.question: What is the best advice to an HIV-positive mother to avoid transmission to her baby?
questions.exp: Maternal ART with suppressed viral load is the main prevention.

questions.question: A boy injured playing football has leg pain and cannot bear weight; X-ray shows a flat femoral epiphysis (slipped). What is the best management?
questions.exp: SCFE: in-situ screw fixation.

questions.question: A baby's mother has hepatitis B. When can the vaccine be given alone without HBIG?
questions.exp: HBIG plus vaccine for babies of HBsAg-positive mothers (especially HBeAg-positive); vaccine alone if all negative.
questions.c: Mother is negative for all markers

questions.question: A child has a red papular rash on the face and trunk with fever, consistent with chickenpox. What can happen later?
questions.exp: VZV stays latent in dorsal root ganglia and can reactivate as shingles. SSPE follows measles.

questions.question: A 9-month-old recently switched from breast milk to formula has widespread urticaria with perioral swelling and is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Without airway, breathing or circulation compromise this is a mild reaction to cow's milk: antihistamine and hydrolysed formula. Reviewers were split with adrenaline.

questions.question: A baby boy comes to ER with high RR, distress and low oxygen. What is the best management?
questions.exp: Bronchiolitis: supportive care with oxygen and hydration.

questions.question: A girl has had a URTI and now has leg weakness without sensory involvement. What is the best investigation?
questions.exp: Guillain–Barré: CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation. NCS also confirm it and was not among the remembered options.

questions.question: A child has septic shock (meningococcal septicaemia). What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Fluid boluses and antibiotics first, then inotropes if fluid-refractory.
questions.a: IV adrenaline, intubation, IV antibiotics and IV fluids
questions.c: IV fluids, IV antibiotics, then inotropes through an IV line

questions.question: In coeliac disease, when is a jejunal (duodenal) biopsy needed?
questions.exp: Positive IgA tTG prompts biopsy unless the tTG is very high (no-biopsy pathway).

questions.question: What is the first test when coeliac disease is suspected?
questions.exp: IgA tTG with total IgA is first line.
